title: Disabled phishing link still redirects
description: Your shortener uses 301 Moved Permanently and caches alias lookups in Redis without a TTL. The trust and safety team disables a phishing link: the API sets disabled_at and deletes the Redis key. Hours later, people following the link still reach the phishing page. Which change best fixes the design for revocable links?

options.text: Delete the Redis key twice, with a short delay between deletes, to avoid racing with a concurrent cache fill.
options.explanation: A delayed double delete narrows one race, but browsers that already received a 301 never ask the server again, so the server-side cache is not the main problem.

options.text: Move the link table from read replicas to the primary so the disabled_at flag is always fresh.
options.explanation: A primary read can avoid replica lag, but it cannot help a request that never reaches the service because the browser already cached a permanent redirect.

options.text: Return 302 with a short Cache-Control max-age matching the disable SLA, give cache entries a TTL, and purge any CDN copy on takedown.
options.explanation: A browser can reuse a cached 301 without contacting you. For future redirects, a 302 with bounded max-age, bounded server-side cache freshness and an explicit CDN purge supports revocation. You cannot remotely clear a permanent redirect already stored in someone's browser.

options.text: Rotate the alias to a new random value whenever a link is disabled.
options.explanation: Changing the alias does not affect the old alias that victims already hold; their browsers still follow the cached permanent redirect.
